transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I guess what finally made me agree to come in is that I’ve sort of stopped caring about the things that used to keep me steady. I’m 51, I’ve always been the kind of guy who keeps busy—work, projects, commitments, hobbies—and usually that’s helped me feel like myself.

But lately, even the things I used to genuinely look forward to just feel like chores. Sailing races, for example… I used to plan my week around them, check the weather, mess with gear, all of that. Now I find myself putting it off or making excuses. Same with my Saturday shift at the historical society—I used to enjoy being useful there, talking with people, keeping up with the little routines. And even being out in the woodshop, tinkering with something, which used to calm me down… now it’s like I look at the tools and just think, “Not today.”

It’s not that I suddenly hate any of it. It’s more like the interest got turned way down, and I can’t seem to get it back. That’s what worried me enough to come in.
Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time lately?

Sad, exactly… I don’t know if I’d call it that most of the time. It’s not like I’m walking around crying or feeling openly miserable all day.

It’s more this constant low-level dread, if that makes sense. Like there’s this weight in the background, and it keeps turning into guilt. I keep thinking I should have seen one more thing coming, one more risk, one more problem before it happened. And people tell me, “The controls were in place, you did what you were supposed to do,” but it doesn’t really land. I can hear that logically, but emotionally it just sort of bounces off.

So empty, maybe… but mostly it feels like dread and guilt following me around, even when there’s no immediate reason for it right in front of me.
Have you noticed a decrease in pleasure from activities you used to enjoy?

Yes… definitely. That’s probably the clearest thing I can point to, honestly.

It’s not like I made some decision to stop doing things. It’s more that the enjoyment just sort of drained out of them. Sailing races used to be a big thing for me—I’d look forward to them, think about the weather, the equipment, who’d be there, all the little details. Now I catch myself treating it like one more obligation, like something I need an excuse to get out of.

Same with my Saturday shift at the historical society. I used to like being part of that routine, feeling useful, talking to people. Lately I’ll look at it on the calendar and just feel this… heaviness, like, “Do I really have to go?”

And the woodshop too. That used to be the place I could kind of settle myself. I’d tinker, fix something, make little adjustments. Now I’ll stand there looking at the tools and I just don’t have the pull toward it. It all feels like chores I keep putting off, even though these were the things that used to keep me balanced.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep lately?

Yes, my sleep’s been different. I can usually make myself go to bed at a reasonable time — I’m not up all night pacing or anything like that — but staying asleep is the problem.

Most nights I wake up around two or three in the morning, and it’s like my mind is suddenly right back on that job site. I’ll be half-awake at first, and then all the details start coming back, and once that starts I’m just… up. I’ll lie there trying not to think about it, but that never really works.

And then I get very aware of sounds in the house or outside. The furnace clicking on, a car going by, a board creaking — little normal noises, I know that, but at that hour they feel louder than they should. So instead of getting real rest, I’m lying there listening, waiting, trying to settle myself back down. Some nights I eventually doze off again, but it doesn’t feel like good sleep.
How long have you been feeling this way?

It’s been… a little over a year now, I think. It started after the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period.

At first I kept telling myself it was just stress from everything changing at work, and that once things settled down I’d settle down too. But it didn’t really fade the way I expected. It’s been there in one form or another since then, not necessarily at the same intensity every single day, but enough that I can’t honestly say it ever went back to normal.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past year?

I don’t think so, no. Not a significant amount, anyway.

I mean, my clothes don’t really fit differently, and nobody’s said anything like I look thinner. I haven’t been tracking my weight closely, so I can’t give you an exact number, but I don’t have the sense that I’ve lost a lot over the past year. If anything, it’s probably been more or less the same.
Do you often find yourself worrying about things that might happen in the future?

I’m not sure I’d say I’m constantly worrying about the future, no. I mean, I think about practical things like anyone does — work, money, family stuff, what needs to get done — but I don’t know that I sit around imagining every possible bad thing that could happen.

It’s more that when something specific is in front of me, I can get caught up in it a bit. But just in general, worrying about the future all the time… I haven’t really noticed that as the main issue.
Have you been having thoughts about death or dying?

Death or dying… I don’t know. Not in the sense of making plans or wanting to die, no. I wouldn’t say that.

I mean, thoughts can come up in a more general way, like when something reminds me how things can go wrong suddenly, and then I’ll think about mortality or how fragile things are. But I don’t sit there thinking I’d be better off dead, if that’s what you mean. It’s more… unsettling thoughts, not something I’m seeking out or wanting.
Have you had any thoughts about hurting yourself?

No, I haven’t had thoughts about hurting myself.

I mean, I don’t want to make it sound like everything is fine all the time, because I do get upset or overwhelmed sometimes, but hurting myself specifically… no. I haven’t been thinking about doing that, and I don’t have any plan or intention like that. If anything, when I get shaken up, I’m more trying to get through the moment than thinking about harming myself.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly or feeling like you're speeding up in your thoughts or actions lately?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed that, honestly. I mean, I don’t think I’ve been moving unusually slowly, like people are commenting on it or I feel like I’m physically dragging in some obvious way. And I don’t think I’ve been sped up either, like talking a mile a minute or unable to sit still because my body is racing.

My thoughts can feel busy at times, but I wouldn’t describe it as “sped up” exactly. It’s more just… normal stress or trying to sort through things. But in terms of what you’re asking — moving slower or everything speeding up — no, I don’t think that’s been a big thing I’ve noticed lately.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

Yeah… that’s actually a big part of why I finally agreed to come in.

I still know, intellectually, what I used to enjoy. Like sailing races — those used to be one of the things that kept me feeling like myself. I’d look forward to them, check the weather, think through the route, all of that. And my Saturday shift with the historical society used to feel meaningful, like a nice anchor in the week. Even being out in the woodshop, just tinkering with something, sanding or adjusting a piece until it was right… that was usually calming for me.

But lately it’s more like I look at those things and they feel like obligations. Chores. I keep putting them off, or I tell myself I’ll get back to them next weekend, and then I don’t. It’s not that I hate them now, exactly. I just don’t seem to care in the same way. The anticipation isn’t there. I don’t get that little lift from thinking about them. And that bothers me, because those were the things that used to keep me balanced.
Would you say your feelings of dread and guilt are interfering with your daily life most of the time, or is it more intermittent?

Most of the time, I think. Not every single second, but it’s there in the background a lot.

It’s like this low-grade dread and guilt that follows me around during the day. I keep feeling like I should have seen one more risk coming, or caught one more thing before it became a problem, even though people keep telling me the controls were in place and that I did what I was supposed to do. I can hear that logically, but it doesn’t really settle it emotionally.

So it’s not always dramatic, like I’m visibly falling apart all day. I can still get through things. But it’s there enough that it colors a lot of my normal routines. I’ll be doing something ordinary and then that feeling comes back — like I missed something, like I should have anticipated more — and it’s hard to just move on from it.
Would you say the dread and guilt are overwhelming at times or are they more of a persistent, manageable feeling?

It’s more persistent than overwhelming, I’d say. I mean, there are moments where it feels heavier, where it kind of rises up and I get stuck on it, but most of the time it’s not like I’m completely incapacitated by it.

It’s more like this constant low-grade dread and guilt sitting in the background. Like I’m going through the day and some part of me is still reviewing everything, thinking, “You should have seen one more risk. You should have caught one more thing.” And the frustrating part is that people keep telling me the controls were in place, that it wasn’t because I ignored something or failed to do what I was supposed to do. I can repeat that back to myself, but it doesn’t really make the feeling go away.

So… manageable, technically, yes. I can function. But persistent. It follows me around more than I’d like to admit.
Have you had periods of feeling depressed like this before?

I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly.

I mean, I’ve had bad stretches before, sure — stressful projects, family stuff, times where I was tired or discouraged or not enjoying things as much for a while. I don’t think I’d call those the same as this, though. Or at least I don’t remember them having this same kind of weight to them.

Part of me wants to say no, not like this. But then I wonder if I’m minimizing earlier periods because I got through them and moved on. I’ve always been the sort of person who just keeps functioning and tells myself it’s just a rough patch. So I don’t know if I’ve ever really stopped and labeled it as “depressed.”

But as far as I can tell, this feels different enough that it’s what got my attention. It’s not just being in a slump for a week or two. It feels more persistent, more tied into everything. So… I guess my best answer is, not that I can clearly remember in this same way.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to, even if it's just a little bit?

Not really, no. I mean… maybe tiny moments here and there, but nothing I actually look forward to the way I used to.

That’s honestly part of what finally made me agree to come in. I used to have things that kind of kept me balanced. Sailing races, for one. I’d plan around them, check conditions, fuss with gear, talk strategy — even if I was busy, I wanted to be there. And my Saturday shift at the historical society used to feel meaningful, like a quiet thing I did that connected me to something outside of work. Even tinkering in the woodshop — that was always my way of decompressing.

Now all of that just feels like… chores. Things I keep putting off. I’ll tell myself I should go, or I should get out to the shop for an hour, and then I just don’t. Or if I do, I’m kind of going through the motions and waiting until I can leave. It’s not that I hate those things now. I just don’t seem to care about them the way I did, and that worries me.
How long have you been feeling this persistent low-grade dread and guilt?

It really started after the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period. I keep trying to pin it down like there was a specific day it began, but it’s more like… after that happened, it just never fully lifted.

So, a little over a year now, I guess. Which sounds strange to say out loud, because for a while I kept treating it like it was just the aftermath of a bad incident, something that would settle down once the project stabilized or once enough time had passed. But it’s been more than a year, and that low-grade dread and guilt have kind of stayed there in the background the whole time.
Have your symptoms of low pleasure, dread, and guilt lasted for at least two weeks at any point over the past year?

Yes. Definitely at least two weeks. I mean, it’s been much longer than that.

It’s been going on since the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period afterward. I kept thinking it would ease up once things got reorganized or once I got some distance from it, but it didn’t really go away. It’s more like it settled in and became this background state.

So yes, over the past year there have absolutely been stretches longer than two weeks where the low pleasure, the dread, and the guilt were just… there. Honestly, it’s been a little over a year now.
Have your symptoms of low pleasure, dread, and guilt been present for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks at any point over the past year?

Yes… yes, I’d say so. I know I’ve kind of already said it’s been longer than two weeks, but the “most of the day, nearly every day” part — yeah, that fits too, unfortunately.

It’s not like I only feel it for an hour and then I’m fine. Since the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period afterward, it’s been sort of woven into the day. Some days it’s quieter, I guess, more in the background, but it’s still there. I’ll be at work or at home or trying to do something normal, and it’s just this low hum of dread or guilt, and the lack of pleasure in things is there too.

So yes, at some point over this past year — really, for a little over a year now — it’s been present most of the day, nearly every day, for much longer than two weeks.
Have your symptoms of low pleasure, dread, and guilt been present for at least two years?

No, not two years. It feels like it’s been a long time, and honestly some days it feels longer than it actually has been, but if I’m being accurate, it’s been a little over a year.

It started after the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period. That’s when the low pleasure and the dread and guilt really set in and just… stayed. I think because the readjustment dragged on and everything around it kept reminding me of what happened, it makes the timeline feel stretched out in my head.

But no, I wouldn’t say two years. More like just over a year now.
Have your symptoms of low pleasure, dread, and guilt been present for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks in a row at any point?

Yes. I know I’ve said pieces of this already, but yes — there have definitely been periods where it was most of the day, nearly every day, for more than two weeks in a row.

It really started after the scaffold accident, during the business readjustment afterward. At first I kept thinking, okay, this is just the immediate aftermath, I just need to get through the next set of changes or the next work adjustment. But it didn’t really lift. It stayed with me day after day, and now it’s been a little over a year. So, yes, that two-weeks-in-a-row part definitely applies.

target_item.reason: The question asks about whether there were prior periods of depression before the current symptoms, but the provided symptom profile does not include past depressive episodes or psychiatric history.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that cleanly.

I mean, I’ve had bad stretches before, sure — stressful projects, family stuff, times where I was tired or discouraged or not enjoying things as much for a while. I don’t think I’d call those the same as this, though. Or at least I don’t remember them having this same kind of weight to them.

Part of me wants to say no, not like this. But then I wonder if I’m minimizing earlier periods because I got through them and moved on. I’ve always been the sort of person who just keeps functioning and tells myself it’s just a rough patch. So I don’t know if I’ve ever really stopped and labeled it as “depressed.”

But as far as I can tell, this feels different enough that it’s what got my attention. It’s not just being in a slump for a week or two. It feels more persistent, more tied into everything. So… I guess my best answer is, not that I can clearly remember in this same way.

inference.note: F32.0 and F33.0 were ruled out due to the duration and persistence of symptoms

doctor.intent: determine the presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to, even if it's just a little bit?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: What finally made me agree to come in is that I just don't care about the things that used to keep me balanced—sailing races, my Saturday historical society shift, even tinkering in the woodshop all feel like chores I keep putting off.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether I still experience pleasure or anticipation in activities, which directly concerns diminished interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed activities.

patient.answer:
Not really, no. I mean… maybe tiny moments here and there, but nothing I actually look forward to the way I used to.

That’s honestly part of what finally made me agree to come in. I used to have things that kind of kept me balanced. Sailing races, for one. I’d plan around them, check conditions, fuss with gear, talk strategy — even if I was busy, I wanted to be there. And my Saturday shift at the historical society used to feel meaningful, like a quiet thing I did that connected me to something outside of work. Even tinkering in the woodshop — that was always my way of decompressing.

Now all of that just feels like… chores. Things I keep putting off. I’ll tell myself I should go, or I should get out to the shop for an hour, and then I just don’t. Or if I do, I’m kind of going through the motions and waiting until I can leave. It’s not that I hate those things now. I just don’t seem to care about them the way I did, and that worries me.

doctor.intent: determine the duration of the patient's current depressive episode
doctor.question: How long have you been feeling this persistent low-grade dread and guilt?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since the scaffold accident during the business readjustment, a little over a year now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the persistent low-grade dread and guilt have been present, which is directly about symptom duration.

patient.answer:
It really started after the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period. I keep trying to pin it down like there was a specific day it began, but it’s more like… after that happened, it just never fully lifted.

So, a little over a year now, I guess. Which sounds strange to say out loud, because for a while I kept treating it like it was just the aftermath of a bad incident, something that would settle down once the project stabilized or once enough time had passed. But it’s been more than a year, and that low-grade dread and guilt have kind of stayed there in the background the whole time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the duration criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have your symptoms of low pleasure, dread, and guilt lasted for at least two weeks at any point over the past year?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since the scaffold accident during the business readjustment, a little over a year now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the symptoms have lasted and whether they persisted for at least two weeks, which is most directly covered by the duration profile.

patient.answer:
Yes. Definitely at least two weeks. I mean, it’s been much longer than that.

It’s been going on since the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period afterward. I kept thinking it would ease up once things got reorganized or once I got some distance from it, but it didn’t really go away. It’s more like it settled in and became this background state.

So yes, over the past year there have absolutely been stretches longer than two weeks where the low pleasure, the dread, and the guilt were just… there. Honestly, it’s been a little over a year now.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms meet the duration criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have your symptoms of low pleasure, dread, and guilt been present for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks at any point over the past year?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since the scaffold accident during the business readjustment, a little over a year now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the time course and persistence of the symptoms over the past year, which is most directly covered by the duration item.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I’d say so. I know I’ve kind of already said it’s been longer than two weeks, but the “most of the day, nearly every day” part — yeah, that fits too, unfortunately.

It’s not like I only feel it for an hour and then I’m fine. Since the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period afterward, it’s been sort of woven into the day. Some days it’s quieter, I guess, more in the background, but it’s still there. I’ll be at work or at home or trying to do something normal, and it’s just this low hum of dread or guilt, and the lack of pleasure in things is there too.

So yes, at some point over this past year — really, for a little over a year now — it’s been present most of the day, nearly every day, for much longer than two weeks.

doctor.intent: determine if symptoms meet the duration criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have your symptoms of low pleasure, dread, and guilt been present for at least two years?

target_item.name: Duration

target_item.reason: The doctor's question is asking about how long the symptoms have been present, specifically whether they have lasted at least two years.

patient.answer:
No, not two years. It feels like it’s been a long time, and honestly some days it feels longer than it actually has been, but if I’m being accurate, it’s been a little over a year.

It started after the scaffold accident, during that whole business readjustment period. That’s when the low pleasure and the dread and guilt really set in and just… stayed. I think because the readjustment dragged on and everything around it kept reminding me of what happened, it makes the timeline feel stretched out in my head.

But no, I wouldn’t say two years. More like just over a year now.
